channel.title: Quant Arena
channel.description: Weekly arena reports, research articles and site updates.

item.title: Quant Arena Weekly Report: week 2026-W46 (2026-11-09 – 2026-11-13)
item.description: What moved in the arena during the week ending 2026-11-13: market moves, strategies that changed position, and the best and worst performers over the last month.

item.title: Does the 200-Day Moving Average Rule Work? Ten Markets Tested
item.description: Holding only while price is above its 200-day average had a smaller maximum drawdown than buy-and-hold in all ten markets and a higher Sharpe ratio in nine, but it trailed on return in US stocks, gold and bitcoin and switched 1,140 times in total, before costs.

item.title: Does Buying the Dip Work? Four Dip Rules on Ten Markets
item.description: After a fall of 3% or more in five days, inside an uptrend, the average 21-day return was +1.0% against +0.7% on all days (medians over nine markets, 2010-2026): higher in 8 of 9 markets but statistically clear in only one, and the worst case, US stocks on 2020-02-24, lost 24.1% over the next 21 days.

item.title: How Did 61 Strategies Handle the 2020 COVID Crash on US Stocks?
item.description: In the site's replay of 19 February to 23 March 2020, US stocks (SPY) fell 33.7%. Only 3 of 61 strategies made money, though 58 did better than buy-and-hold, but 38 were flat at the low and just 3 recaptured half of the 39.9% rebound that followed.

item.title: 60/40, All Weather, Dual Momentum: 22 Famous Rules Replicated
item.description: Replicated on the site's markets since 2010, the best return per unit of drawdown among the 22 famous portfolios and rules came from a Stage 2 trend rule (0.89), but without its bitcoin slot it falls to 0.39. The fixed-weight 60/40-style, All Weather-style and 90/10 mixes all landed at 0.41 to 0.42, the same as holding SPY.

item.title: Golden Cross and Death Cross Tested on Ten Markets
item.description: A long-only 50/200 moving-average rule beat buy-and-hold on return in 7 of 10 markets and cut the maximum drawdown in 9, but it did not help US stocks, gold or bitcoin, and no market showed a statistically clear edge after either cross (107 golden and 106 death crosses in total, before costs).

item.title: Which Trading Sayings Hold Up? A Scorecard of 34 Claims
item.description: Of 34 popular trading sayings tested on up to ten markets (2010-2026, before costs), 1 holds, 11 partly hold, 19 do not hold and 3 lack data; most of the survivors describe risk, not a way to predict returns.

item.title: Do Trend Followers Exit Before Stock Crashes? 12 Events Tested
item.description: Across 12 US stock sell-offs in the site's event replays, trend strategies were already out when the fall began only 29.9% of the time on average, less often than on a normal day (38.6%). They still lost just 4.7% against the market's 15.0%, because they left during the fall.

item.title: What Follows High Volatility? 21-Day Returns in 10 Markets
item.description: After high-volatility days, the next 21 days beat the market's own average in 5 of 10 markets and lagged it in the other 5, and no gap exceeds two standard errors. The one consistent pattern is wider outcomes: 9 of 10 markets had a larger spread of 21-day returns after high volatility.

item.title: 21 research articles: seven filled in, six expanded, eight new
item.description: Seven strategy explainers that had only a title now have full articles written from the code and the backtest data. Six short articles are rewritten at full length with current figures. Eight new ones cover the golden cross, the 200-day rule, buying dips, a scorecard of all tested sayings, the 2020 crash replayed, trend following in crashes, famous portfolios replicated, and what follows each volatility regime. Every figure is recomputed from the site's data.

item.title: Tools page and a VPS partner
item.description: A new Tools page, linked from the header, lists what we recommend for running these strategies yourself. Expert Advisor pages now carry a labelled affiliate link to a forex VPS provider; it does not affect rankings or results.

item.title: TradingView partner links
item.description: Strategy, code and open-source project pages now carry a labelled TradingView affiliate link, including a button under each Pine Script. We may earn a commission if you subscribe through it; it does not affect rankings or results.

item.title: Strategy code downloads, head-to-head comparisons and a GitHub finance hot list
item.description: Every strategy now has a code page with the Python file the backtests run, free to download and runnable on its own; 55 also have a TradingView Pine Script version (converted by hand, not compiled by us). Strategy vs strategy pages compare the top strategies on each market pair by pair. Finance on GitHub ranks 1,300+ open-source finance and trading projects by stars, refreshed weekly. The home page links to all research tools.

item.title: Ads on reading pages
item.description: Strategy, EA, research, glossary and the new section pages can now show ads: Google AdSense, plus one labelled block near the bottom of the page that loads only when you scroll to it. Evidence, cost, AI season and legal pages stay ad-free. The privacy policy is updated.

item.title: Four new sections: market regimes, claim checker, event replays, famous strategies
item.description: Market regimes shows each market's trend, volatility and strategy positioning every trading day. The claim checker tests 34 popular trading sayings on daily data and gives each a verdict. Event replays show how the strategies behaved in 35 major market events since 2010, plus recent sell-offs detected automatically. Famous strategies re-runs 22 well-known public portfolios and rule sets on our ten markets and says what had to be adapted.

item.title: Optional coffee support for continued research
item.description: An optional Ko-fi link now appears in the footer, at the end of research articles and beside prepared or verified browser downloads. Contributions support data updates, backtest verification and new tools. All existing free downloads remain available. The support provider opens only when you choose the link; no payment widget loads automatically.

item.title: Compare portfolio additions and removals from pinned evidence
item.description: A new comparison worksheet keeps before and after on identical shared dates, separates strategy and allocation fees, and shows gross/net returns, recovery, downside sample counts and signed exposure overlap. Frozen share links retain the original evidence; optional named saves stay in this browser. Independent sleeves do not net trades across strategies. Financing, borrowing, funding, taxes and market impact remain excluded.

item.title: Cost comparisons across 576 supported pairs
item.description: All 576 supported strategy-market pairs now have separate 0, 5, 10 and 25 bp cost scenarios across seven windows. Strategies and matched benchmarks each pay charges on their own drift-adjusted one-way risky turnover after gross returns. Rankings compare identical asset universes, dates, input returns and window anchors; a basket labelled SPY is kept separate from single-market SPY. Fee totals use the disclosed initial-capital or start-close-capital units. Metrics use all original full-precision daily records, while curves are bounded display samples and metrics load by the selected universe. This independent fee-sensitivity view leaves existing before-cost Arena rankings intact. It models synthetic exposure charges, not actual broker fills or exact traded notional; financing, borrow, funding, taxes and market impact remain excluded.

item.title: Common-date AI season scheduled after public freeze
item.description: OpenAI and Anthropic each retain six unchanged rules. Their prompt, original replies and receipt metadata were verified publicly on 7 November 2026 at 00:20 UTC, before scheduling. Season 1 runs from 9 November 2026 through 6 February 2027. It is scheduled, with no performance yet; rankings require at least 20 observations in every required market and complete matching windows. Late entrants belong to a later season.

item.title: Quant Arena Weekly Report: week 2026-W45 (2026-11-02 – 2026-11-06)
item.description: What moved in the arena during the week ending 2026-11-06: market moves, strategies that changed position, and the best and worst performers over the last month.

item.title: Common-date AI seasons: two frozen provider submissions
item.description: Two real CLI submissions, from OpenAI and Anthropic, now retain all six frozen rules each under one public prompt, with exact prompt/reply downloads, requested and reported model fields, freeze timestamps and operator-recorded receipts. The common-date season remains a draft: no start has been scheduled and no performance or rankings are published. Anthropic reports claude-sonnet-5 and discloses auxiliary claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 usage; the auxiliary purpose and underlying model revision are not established, and inference compute is not normalized across providers. The original single-assistant experiment remains separate with its original figures and disclosed execution-timing and rounded-input limitations. These CLI receipts are not provider-signed attestations.

item.title: Full-cohort evidence and causal calendar corrections
item.description: Evidence now covers all 72 strategies and 576 supported pairs, including signed per-asset basket holdings. Daily records, configurations and archived source can be downloaded on demand; the standalone tool can fetch inputs and regenerate rules when the original input fingerprint matches. Every current run has original-input recomputation proof across 2,394,468 observations, including 11 newly corrected runs. Ten monthly basket rules now decide on the first observed new-month session using the preceding observation, with the engine lag retained. The turn-of-month rule uses a disclosed weekday approximation, not an exchange-holiday calendar. These corrections change historical results; old immutable runs and correction links remain available. Costs remain zero in this baseline; synthetic targets and rebalancing are not broker fills.

item.title: Auditable strategy evidence and direct engine positions
item.description: Six representative strategies now have evidence bundles on SPY, gold and bitcoin: full-precision daily accounting, simulated position changes, actual selected parameters, source hashes and a standalone arithmetic replay script. The evidence index preserves prior corrected snapshots. Signals now come from engine targets rather than ratios of rounded returns, with target and effective exposure, per-market observation dates and independent data status. The current UTC date is excluded conservatively. Walk-forward boundary returns are recomputed from the previous published target, and skipped folds retain default targets; the evidence index quantifies these accounting changes. This is an 18-pair pilot, not full-site verification or broker fills.

item.title: New: AI Strategy Arena
item.description: Six trading rules written by an AI assistant, with every parameter fixed, are now tracked every trading day on nine markets against buy-and-hold and our 72 classic strategies. Because a language model may already know past markets, the ranking uses only results after 4 November 2026, the day the rules were frozen; the historical backtest is shown for reference only.

item.title: New: open-source trading frameworks directory
item.description: A guide to 18 widely used open-source projects for backtesting, live trading, crypto bots, machine learning and market data (Backtrader, vectorbt, LEAN, NautilusTrader, vn.py, Freqtrade, Qlib, FinRL, TradingAgents and more): what each is for, strengths, limitations, alternatives and seven head-to-head comparisons. GitHub stars, last commit, latest release and maintenance status are refreshed every week.

item.title: We Backtested 72 Strategies. After Adjusting for Luck, None Clearly Beat the Odds.
item.description: 104 strategy-and-market combinations look statistically convincing on their own. Once you account for the fact that we tested hundreds of them at the same time, the number drops to zero. Here is what that means for reading any leaderboard, including ours.

item.title: We Tried to Backtest 1,063 Free MT5 Expert Advisors. Here Is What Survived.
item.description: Free MetaTrader 5 EAs from the MQL5 CodeBase, converted automatically and tested on four markets for one year. More than half could not be converted at all. Of the 1,123 results we trust, about half made money — but on currencies the typical EA ended flat, only 30 EAs were profitable on all four markets, and one in five gold runs wiped out the account.

item.title: Which Strategies Survived 2022, and Did the Winners Keep Winning?
item.description: In calendar 2022 US stocks fell 18.2% and only 10 of 55 single-market strategies finished positive, 8 of them mean-reversion rules. In 2023 those ten all stayed positive, yet their median return was 3.7% against 14.8% for the rest, and the rank correlation between the two years was −0.58.

item.title: Why Martingale and Grid EAs Blow Up: What 1,515 Free MT5 Expert Advisors and Their Losing Streaks Show
item.description: Martingale and grid EAs make up 5% of the free MT5 Expert Advisors we review, but more than half of the ones we rate "dangerous". The reason is arithmetic: losing streaks of six to eight trades are normal — and that is exactly where doubling the position runs out of money.

item.title: Do Moving-Average Strategies Beat Buy-and-Hold on Bitcoin?
item.description: Over the last five years six moving-average systems all had a shallower maximum drawdown than holding bitcoin (−36.7% to −51.2% against −75.9%), and four beat its 2.6% annual return. Over the full history since September 2014 only one of six beat holding on return (MACD, 59.0% against 52.0%).

item.title: Does Turtle Trading Still Work? Ten Markets, 2021–2026
item.description: Over the five years to November 2026 the 20/10 Turtle breakout (TURTLE-01) made 6.0% a year on US stocks against 11.9% for holding, with a smaller drawdown (-13.3% against -24.5%). It beat holding on return on four of ten markets, and the slower Donchian Breakout (TREND-02) had the higher return and Sharpe ratio on eight.

item.title: Does an RSI Filter Improve MACD? A Ten-Market Backtest
item.description: Adding an RSI filter to a MACD crossover (COMBO-02 against TREND-12) cut trades on all ten markets and the five-year maximum drawdown on nine, but raised the Sharpe ratio on only six. The filter kept the strategy invested on 33% of days instead of 50%, and it cost the most return on bitcoin.

item.title: Same Max Drawdown, Different Pain: Ulcer Index and Rolling Sharpe
item.description: On US stocks over the last five years, Z-Score Mean Reversion and Volatility Breakout both had a maximum drawdown of about 10% (−10.4% and −10.1%), yet one spent at most 224 days below its previous high and the other 1,006, and their Ulcer indexes were 1.3% and 5.4%.

item.title: Keltner Breakout vs Bollinger Reversion: Ten Markets Compared
item.description: A Keltner Channel breakout and a Bollinger Band reversion rule were never in the market on the same day across ten markets (0 overlapping days out of 4,648 for the reversion rule). Over five years each had the better Sharpe ratio on five markets; over the full history the breakout was ahead on all ten.

item.title: Quant Arena Weekly Report: week 2026-W33 (2026-08-10 – 2026-08-14)
item.description: What moved in the arena during the week ending 2026-08-14: market moves, strategies that changed position, and the best and worst performers over the last month.

item.title: Donchian 55/20 vs Turtle 20/10: A Ten-Market Backtest
item.description: Before trading costs, the slow Donchian Breakout (TREND-02, 55-day high in, 20-day low out) made 774 entries across ten markets against 1,979 for Turtle Trading (TURTLE-01, 20/10), and had the higher full-period Sharpe ratio on seven of the ten markets (mean 0.38 vs 0.34). Over the last five years the gap was wider: 0.41 vs 0.21.

item.title: Supertrend vs ATR Trailing Stop vs Chandelier Exit: Backtested
item.description: Supertrend (SUPER-01), the ATR trailing stop (RISK-04) and Chandelier Exit (TREND-17) ended with almost the same average full-period Sharpe ratio (0.38, 0.41 and 0.40) before trading costs, but they entered the market 1,973, 4,852 and 8,320 times. Much of the difference is how quickly each one re-enters after an exit.

item.title: Ichimoku Cloud vs a 50/200 Moving Average: Ten-Market Test
item.description: Before trading costs, the Ichimoku Cloud (TREND-10) as coded here had a higher full-period Sharpe ratio than the 50/200 Dual Moving Average (TREND-05) on six of ten markets and a shallower maximum drawdown on eight (mean −39.4% vs −50.4%), but it made 1,460 entries against 218.

item.title: Does Buying When RSI Is Below 30 Work? A Ten-Market Backtest
item.description: RSI Mean Reversion (MR-01) is long only on days when RSI is below 30; the code never holds a position until RSI recovers. That left it invested on 5.9% of days on US stocks over five years, with a 5.2% annual return and a 7.2% maximum drawdown, against 11.9% and 24.5% for holding.

item.title: EMA Crossover Strategy: Reading Trend With Two Clocks
item.description: An in depth look at why exponential moving average crossovers persist, how to interpret their backtests, and when trend signals fail.
